title: MasterChef Winner Pankaj Bhadouria Urges Women to Get Regular Cancer Screenings
excerpt: Celebrity chef Pankaj Bhadouria, diagnosed with breast cancer in May, is now undergoing chemotherapy and has called on women — especially those in their 40s — to prioritize routine health check-ups.
body:
• MasterChef India Season 1 winner Pankaj Bhadouria was diagnosed with breast cancer in May 2026 and underwent surgery on May 29.
  • Early detection through a routine health check-up caught the cancer at an early stage, making her surgery successful.
  • Post-surgery biopsies revealed a HER2-positive invasive component, requiring 12 chemotherapy sessions and one year of targeted therapy.
  • Bhadouria has appealed to women in their 40s to get regular breast cancer screenings, noting that one in 20 Indian women is susceptible to the disease.

Celebrity chef and India's first MasterChef winner Pankaj Bhadouria has turned her breast cancer diagnosis into a public campaign for women's health awareness, urging women across India and the diaspora to stop delaying routine screenings.

Bhadouria, 55, revealed on May 28 that she had been diagnosed with breast cancer, sharing a photo from her hospital bed. "I have been diagnosed with Breast Cancer. Need your prayers and support," she wrote. Surgery followed the next day, on May 29, and doctors initially told her she could return to work within four weeks.

Early Detection Made the Difference

In a video message posted after her surgery, Bhadouria credited a routine health check-up for catching the cancer before it progressed. "I was very fortunate that my cancer was detected at a very early stage. That is why I could recover. That is why my surgery went so well," she said.

The former MasterChef winner used her platform to speak directly to women in their 40s, a demographic she said often neglects preventive care. "My doctors tell me that in India, one out of every 20 women is susceptible to breast cancer. So please take care of yourself. Be aware of yourself. We all think that it won't happen to us, but it can happen to anyone," she said.

"We all think that it won't happen to us, but it can happen to anyone."

— Pankaj Bhadouria, MasterChef India Season 1 winner

A Longer Road Than Expected

The initial relief of a successful surgery gave way to a harder reality. On June 25, Bhadouria shared a follow-up video revealing that detailed post-surgery biopsies had found a 2mm invasive component that tested HER2-positive — a protein that promotes cancer cell growth.

The finding meant her treatment was far from over. She now faces 12 sessions of chemotherapy and one year of targeted therapy. "It seems I'm back to square one. And I'll have to start all over again," she said, admitting the word chemotherapy left her "a little scared."

But the chef struck a defiant tone: "I am going to take this just like I tackle all my other problems. One day at a time. One dish at a time. The kitchen is not closed yet, my friends. There are many recipes and tips left."

From English Teacher to India's First MasterChef

Bhadouria's career arc itself is a story of reinvention. Before entering the culinary world, she spent 16 years as an English teacher. She left that career to compete on MasterChef India, winning its inaugural season in 2010 and becoming a household name.

She went on to host multiple cooking shows including Chef Pankaj Ka Zayka, Kifayati Kitchen, and 3 Course with Pankaj. She has also built a substantial digital following, with millions of viewers on YouTube and social media platforms where she shares recipes and kitchen tips.

A Wake-Up Call for the Diaspora

Bhadouria's diagnosis resonates particularly with Indian women in the United States and abroad, where cultural reluctance around discussing cancer and preventive health persists. Studies have shown that South Asian women in the US have lower rates of breast cancer screening compared to other demographic groups, often due to stigma, lack of awareness, or competing family priorities.

Dr. Akhila Bomma Reddy, a surgical oncologist at TGH Onco Life Cancer Centre, echoed Bhadouria's message. "Breast cancer is one of the most common cancers among women. However, with timely diagnosis and appropriate treatment, many patients can recover completely," she said. Dr. Reddy recommended that women over 20 perform monthly self-examinations and get mammograms every one to two years as advised by their doctors.

"When breast cancer is diagnosed at an early stage, treatment outcomes are generally much better. Awareness and regular screening remain some of the most effective preventive measures."

— Dr. Akhila Bomma Reddy, Surgical Oncologist

What Women Should Know

Health experts advise watching for warning signs: lumps in the breast, changes in skin texture, nipple discharge, or changes in breast size or shape. Risk factors include age, family history, obesity, and lack of physical activity.

Bhadouria's openness about her diagnosis — from the hospital bed photo to the candid admission of fear about chemotherapy — has already prompted conversations on social media about normalizing cancer discussions. For a public figure in the Indian culinary world to speak this frankly is still rare, and that is precisely why it matters.
